question: What is the difference between var, let, and const?
directAnswer: All three declare variables, but they differ in scope and reassignment. var is function-scoped and can be redeclared, which often causes bugs. let is block-scoped and can be reassigned but not redeclared in the same scope. const is also block-scoped but cannot be reassigned after its initial value. In modern code you should prefer const by default and use let only when you truly need to reassign.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Originally JavaScript only had var, which is function-scoped and gets 'hoisted' in confusing ways. This led to a lot of accidental bugs, especially inside loops and if-blocks. ES6 (2015) introduced let and const to give developers proper block scoping and a way to signal that a value should not change, making code safer and easier to read.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: var declarations are hoisted to the top of their function and initialized as undefined, so you can reference them before the line they appear on. let and const are also hoisted but live in a 'temporal dead zone' until the declaration runs, so accessing them early throws an error. const prevents reassignment of the binding itself, though if it holds an object you can still mutate the object's properties.

whyImportant: This is one of the most common opening questions in any JavaScript interview because it reveals whether you understand scoping, hoisting, and modern best practices. Picking the right keyword prevents a whole class of subtle bugs, so interviewers use it to gauge your day-to-day coding discipline.
realWorldExample: Imagine a for-loop that creates click handlers for buttons. With var, every handler ends up referencing the same final loop value because var is shared across the whole function. Switching to let gives each iteration its own block-scoped copy, so each button correctly logs its own index. This exact bug shows up constantly in real codebases.

nestedTopics.title: Block scope vs function scope
nestedTopics.explanation: let and const only exist inside the nearest pair of curly braces (a block), such as inside an if-statement or loop. var ignores blocks entirely and is visible throughout the whole function it sits in. Block scope is more predictable and is the main reason to avoid var.

nestedTopics.title: const does not mean immutable
nestedTopics.explanation: const only stops you from reassigning the variable to a new value. If the variable points to an object or array, you can still change what is inside it. For example, const arr = []; arr.push(1) is perfectly legal because you are mutating, not reassigning.

nestedTopics.title: Redeclaration rules
nestedTopics.explanation: You can redeclare the same var name multiple times in one scope with no error, which can mask mistakes. Trying to redeclare a let or const in the same scope throws a SyntaxError, which catches accidental duplicate declarations early.

followUps.question: If const cannot be changed, why can I push to a const array?
followUps.answer: Because const protects the binding, not the contents. The variable is locked to point at one specific array in memory, but the array object itself is mutable. Pushing, popping, or editing elements changes the contents while the binding still points at the same array, so it is allowed. If you want truly unchangeable data, you would need something like Object.freeze, which prevents adding or changing properties.

followUps.question: Which one should you use by default and why?
followUps.answer: Use const by default. It communicates that the value is not meant to change, which makes code easier to reason about, and it prevents accidental reassignment bugs. Only switch to let when you genuinely need to reassign the variable, such as a counter or an accumulator. There is almost never a good reason to use var in modern code.

followUps.question: What is the temporal dead zone?
followUps.answer: The temporal dead zone is the period between when a let or const variable enters scope and when its declaration line actually runs. During that window the variable exists but cannot be accessed; touching it throws a ReferenceError. This behavior is intentional, because it forces you to declare variables before using them, unlike var which silently returns undefined when accessed early.

question: What are the primitive data types in JavaScript?
directAnswer: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, and bigint. Everything else, like objects, arrays, and functions, is a non-primitive (reference) type. Primitives are immutable and compared by value, while objects are compared by reference.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
A primitive is the simplest kind of value, one that is not an object and has no methods of its own. Examples:
let name = 'Sara';      // string
let age = 30;           // number
let active = true;      // boolean
let nothing = null;     // null
let x;                  // undefined
The two newer ones, symbol and bigint, cover unique identifiers and very large integers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Every language needs a set of basic building blocks to represent text, numbers, and true/false logic. JavaScript groups these into primitives because they behave differently from objects: they are lightweight, immutable, and copied by value, which keeps simple data fast and predictable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When you assign a primitive to a variable, the actual value is stored directly. When you copy it to another variable, you get an independent copy. Objects work differently: the variable stores a reference (a pointer) to a location in memory, so two variables can point at the same object. Although primitives have no methods, JavaScript temporarily wraps them in object form when you call something like 'hello'.toUpperCase().

whyImportant: Understanding the difference between primitive and reference types explains some of the most common surprises in JavaScript, like why comparing two objects with === can be false even when they look identical, or why copying an array does not behave like copying a number. Interviewers ask this to make sure you grasp how values are stored and compared.
realWorldExample: Suppose you copy a user's age into a new variable and change it; the original is untouched because numbers are copied by value. But if you copy a user object and change a property, the original also changes because both variables point to the same object. Knowing this prevents accidental data corruption in shared state.

nestedTopics.title: Primitives are immutable
nestedTopics.explanation: You cannot change a primitive value itself. When you do something like a string method that 'modifies' a string, JavaScript actually returns a brand new string and leaves the original unchanged. The variable can be reassigned to that new value, but the old value was never altered.

nestedTopics.title: Value vs reference comparison
nestedTopics.explanation: Primitives are compared by their actual value, so 5 === 5 is true. Objects are compared by reference, meaning two separate objects with identical contents are not equal because they live at different memory locations. Only two variables pointing to the very same object are ===.

nestedTopics.title: The newer primitives: symbol and bigint
nestedTopics.explanation: Symbol creates guaranteed-unique values often used as hidden object keys. BigInt represents integers larger than the normal number type can safely hold, written with an n suffix like 9007199254740993n. Both were added later to cover specialized needs.

followUps.question: Is an array a primitive type?
followUps.answer: No. An array is a special kind of object, so it is a reference type, not a primitive. That is why arrays are compared by reference and why typeof on an array returns 'object'. To specifically check for an array you use Array.isArray(value) rather than typeof.

followUps.question: Why does typeof null return 'object'?
followUps.answer: This is a long-standing bug from the very first version of JavaScript that was never fixed because too much existing code depends on it. null is genuinely a primitive representing intentional emptiness, but typeof null returns 'object'. To check for null you should compare directly with === null instead of relying on typeof.

followUps.question: How do primitives have methods if they are not objects?
followUps.answer: When you call a method on a primitive, like 'abc'.length or (5).toFixed(2), JavaScript temporarily wraps the primitive in a corresponding object (String, Number, and so on), runs the method, and then discards the wrapper. This is called autoboxing. It gives primitives convenient methods without making them full objects.

question: What is the difference between == and === ?
directAnswer: Both compare values, but == performs type coercion while === does not. The double-equals operator converts the operands to a common type before comparing, so '5' == 5 is true. The triple-equals operator checks both value and type, so '5' === 5 is false. As a rule, you should use === almost always to avoid surprising coercion bugs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
These are JavaScript's two equality operators. A quick contrast:
'5' == 5     // true  (string is coerced to number)
'5' === 5    // false (different types)
0 == false   // true  (both coerced)
0 === false  // false (number vs boolean)
The loose operator (==) is forgiving about types, the strict operator (===) is not.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JavaScript was designed to be beginner-friendly, so == was created to let values of different types compare equal when they 'look' the same. Over time this proved error-prone, so === was provided to give predictable, type-aware comparisons. Today the strict operator is the recommended default.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When you use ==, JavaScript follows a set of coercion rules: if the types differ, it converts one or both operands (for example, strings to numbers, booleans to numbers) and then compares. With ===, if the types are not identical, it immediately returns false without any conversion, then compares the actual values only when the types already match.

whyImportant: Loose equality is one of the most notorious sources of bugs in JavaScript because its coercion rules are unintuitive. Interviewers ask this to confirm you understand coercion and follow the safer convention of using ===. Getting it wrong can lead to logic that silently behaves incorrectly.
realWorldExample: Imagine validating a form field where an empty input gives you the string ''. Using == with checks like value == 0 would surprisingly be true because both coerce to falsy values, letting invalid data slip through. Using === keeps the comparison strict and predictable, so empty strings and zeros are treated as the distinct things they are.

nestedTopics.title: Common coercion surprises
nestedTopics.explanation: Loose equality produces results that confuse newcomers, like null == undefined being true, but null == 0 being false, and '' == 0 being true. These come from specific conversion rules that are hard to remember, which is exactly why strict equality is preferred.

nestedTopics.title: When == is acceptable
nestedTopics.explanation: There is one common, defensible use of ==: checking for both null and undefined at once. The expression x == null is true only when x is null or undefined, which is a concise and intentional shortcut some teams allow.

nestedTopics.title: Object.is for edge cases
nestedTopics.explanation: Object.is behaves like === but handles two tricky cases differently: it treats NaN as equal to NaN, and it distinguishes +0 from -0. It is useful when you need precise equality semantics that strict equality does not provide.

followUps.question: Why is NaN === NaN false?
followUps.answer: NaN means 'Not a Number' and represents an invalid numeric result. By the IEEE floating-point standard that JavaScript follows, NaN is defined as not equal to anything, including itself. So NaN === NaN is false. To reliably detect NaN you use Number.isNaN(value) or Object.is(value, NaN) instead of an equality check.

followUps.question: What does 'abc' == true evaluate to?
followUps.answer: It evaluates to false. With loose equality, when comparing a string and a boolean, JavaScript converts the boolean true to the number 1 and tries to convert the string 'abc' to a number, which yields NaN. Since NaN equals nothing, the result is false. This is a good example of how unintuitive coercion can be, reinforcing why === is safer.

followUps.question: Does === ever do any type conversion?
followUps.answer: No. Strict equality never converts types. If the two operands are not already the same type, === returns false immediately. Only when the types match does it compare the actual values. This predictability is the main reason it is the recommended default.

question: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
directAnswer: Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving variable and function declarations to the top of their scope before the code runs. Function declarations are fully hoisted, so you can call them before they appear. var variables are hoisted but initialized as undefined. let and const are hoisted too but stay in a temporal dead zone, so accessing them before declaration throws an error.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Hoisting is a side effect of how the JavaScript engine compiles code: it scans for declarations first to allocate them in memory, then runs the code top to bottom. This lets you, for instance, call helper functions defined lower in a file. It was not a deliberate feature so much as a consequence of the engine's two-phase approach.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Before running, the engine registers all declarations in the current scope. Function declarations get their full definition available immediately. var variables get registered and set to undefined, so referencing them early gives undefined rather than an error. let and const are registered but left uninitialized, so referencing them before the declaration line throws a ReferenceError due to the temporal dead zone.

whyImportant: Hoisting explains a lot of confusing behavior, like why a var prints undefined instead of crashing, or why a let throws an error in the same spot. Interviewers ask about it to verify you understand how the engine prepares and executes code, which underpins scoping and closures.
realWorldExample: A developer references a config variable near the top of a file expecting its value, but it was declared with var lower down. Instead of an error, they silently get undefined, leading to a hard-to-find bug. Knowing hoisting rules helps you immediately recognize and fix this kind of issue.

nestedTopics.title: Function declarations vs function expressions
nestedTopics.explanation: A function declaration (function foo(){}) is fully hoisted and callable before its line. A function expression assigned to a variable (const foo = function(){}) is only hoisted as a variable, so calling it early fails because the variable is not yet assigned the function.

nestedTopics.title: var hoisting pitfalls
nestedTopics.explanation: Because var is hoisted and initialized to undefined, code can run without errors but with wrong values. This often hides typos and logic mistakes, which is a key reason modern code prefers let and const that fail loudly instead.

nestedTopics.title: Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
nestedTopics.explanation: let and const are technically hoisted, but they remain inaccessible from the start of the block until their declaration runs. This gap is the temporal dead zone, and accessing the variable in it throws an error rather than returning undefined.

followUps.question: Are let and const hoisted at all?
followUps.answer: Yes, they are hoisted, but in a different way from var. The engine is aware of them at the top of the block, which is why they shadow outer variables, but it does not initialize them. Until execution reaches the declaration line they sit in the temporal dead zone, and accessing them there throws a ReferenceError. So they are hoisted in name but not usable early.

followUps.question: Can you call a function before it is defined?
followUps.answer: It depends on how the function is defined. A function declaration like function greet(){} is fully hoisted, so you can call it before the line where it appears. A function stored in a variable, like const greet = () => {}, is not callable early because only the variable is hoisted, not its value, so you would get an error. This distinction comes up often in interviews.

followUps.question: Does hoisting move code physically in the file?
followUps.answer: No, nothing is physically moved. Your code stays exactly where you wrote it. Hoisting is just a mental model for describing the engine's two-phase process: it registers declarations during a setup phase, then runs statements in order. The behavior looks as if declarations were moved up, but the source text is unchanged.

question: What is the difference between null and undefined?
directAnswer: Both represent the absence of a value, but in different ways. undefined means a variable has been declared but not assigned a value, which JavaScript sets automatically. null is a value you deliberately assign to indicate 'no value' on purpose. So undefined is usually the system's default, while null is an intentional, developer-set emptiness.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
undefined is the default state of an unassigned variable or a missing object property. null is an explicit empty value you choose to set. For example:
let a;            // undefined automatically
let b = null;     // null intentionally
Objects with a missing key return undefined, while a key set to null returns null.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JavaScript needed a way to represent 'this was never given a value' separately from 'this is intentionally empty'. undefined covers the first case and is produced by the engine, while null lets developers explicitly signal emptiness, for example to reset a variable or indicate a database field has no value.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The engine assigns undefined to declared-but-unassigned variables, missing function arguments, and absent object properties. You never normally assign undefined yourself. null, by contrast, is something you write deliberately. With loose equality null == undefined is true, but with strict equality null === undefined is false because their types differ (object vs undefined).

whyImportant: Mixing up these two leads to bugs and unclear code. Interviewers want to see that you know undefined typically signals 'not set yet' while null signals 'intentionally empty', and that you understand how they compare. This clarity matters when handling API responses, optional values, and defensive checks.
realWorldExample: When fetching a user profile, a field the user never filled in might come back as null from the server to clearly say 'no value here'. Meanwhile, accessing a property your code forgot to set returns undefined. Distinguishing them helps you decide whether data is intentionally blank or accidentally missing.

nestedTopics.title: typeof results differ
nestedTopics.explanation: typeof undefined returns 'undefined', which is correct. typeof null returns 'object', which is a historical bug. Because of this, you check for null by comparing directly with === null rather than relying on typeof.

nestedTopics.title: Default function parameters
nestedTopics.explanation: A default parameter value kicks in only when the argument is undefined, not when it is null. So calling a function with null passes null through, while omitting the argument or passing undefined triggers the default. This is a subtle but important distinction.

nestedTopics.title: JSON handling
nestedTopics.explanation: JSON supports null but not undefined. When you stringify an object, properties set to undefined are dropped entirely, while properties set to null are kept. This affects how data survives serialization to and from APIs.

followUps.question: Why does null == undefined return true but null === undefined return false?
followUps.answer: With loose equality, the language has a special rule that treats null and undefined as equal to each other and to nothing else, so null == undefined is true. With strict equality, the types must match, and null is of type object while undefined is of type undefined, so null === undefined is false. This is a deliberate, well-defined behavior rather than a bug.

followUps.question: Should you ever assign undefined to a variable manually?
followUps.answer: Generally no. undefined is meant to be the engine's signal that something was never set, so manually assigning it muddies that meaning. If you want to explicitly mark something as empty or cleared, assign null instead. Keeping undefined as 'not set' and null as 'intentionally empty' makes your intent clearer to other developers.

followUps.question: What does an uninitialized object property return?
followUps.answer: It returns undefined. If you access a key that does not exist on an object, JavaScript gives you undefined rather than throwing an error. This is why checking 'propertyName in object' or comparing to undefined is a common way to test whether a property was ever set, as opposed to it being explicitly null.

question: What does the typeof operator do?
directAnswer: typeof returns a string describing the type of a value, such as 'number', 'string', 'boolean', 'object', 'function', 'undefined', 'symbol', or 'bigint'. It is the simplest way to check what kind of value you are working with, though it has a couple of quirks, most famously returning 'object' for null.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
typeof is a unary operator placed before a value. Examples:
typeof 42          // 'number'
typeof 'hi'        // 'string'
typeof true        // 'boolean'
typeof undefined   // 'undefined'
typeof function(){} // 'function'
typeof null        // 'object' (a known quirk)
It always produces a lowercase string.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JavaScript is dynamically typed, so a variable can hold any type at any time. typeof gives you a quick, runtime way to inspect what type a value currently is, which is useful for validation, guarding against bad input, and writing flexible functions.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: typeof inspects the internal type tag of a value and returns the corresponding string. Most cases are straightforward, but there are two notable behaviors: typeof null returns 'object' due to a legacy bug, and functions, although technically objects, return 'function' to make them easy to detect. Arrays and other objects all return the generic 'object'.

whyImportant: Type checking is a routine part of writing robust JavaScript, especially when handling user input or data from external sources. Interviewers ask about typeof to ensure you know how to inspect types and that you are aware of its quirks, so you do not write checks that silently misbehave.
realWorldExample: Before performing math on a value that came from a form, you might check typeof value === 'number' to confirm it is actually numeric and not an accidental string. This guard prevents operations like addition from concatenating strings instead of adding numbers, a very common bug source.

nestedTopics.title: Detecting arrays
nestedTopics.explanation: Because typeof returns 'object' for arrays, it cannot distinguish them from plain objects. To reliably check for an array you use Array.isArray(value), which returns a clear true or false. This is the standard, safe approach.

nestedTopics.title: typeof on undeclared variables
nestedTopics.explanation: typeof is uniquely safe on variables that were never declared: typeof someUndeclaredVar returns 'undefined' instead of throwing an error. This makes it handy for feature detection where a variable might not exist at all.

nestedTopics.title: The null quirk
nestedTopics.explanation: typeof null returning 'object' is a long-standing bug that cannot be fixed without breaking the web. Always remember to check for null separately with value === null rather than expecting typeof to identify it.

followUps.question: How do you check if a value is an array?
followUps.answer: Use Array.isArray(value), which returns true only for arrays. You cannot use typeof for this because arrays report as 'object', the same as plain objects and null-free objects. Array.isArray is the clean, purpose-built check and is supported in all modern environments.

followUps.question: What does typeof return for a function?
followUps.answer: It returns 'function'. Even though functions are technically a special kind of object in JavaScript, typeof singles them out with their own result so you can easily verify that a value is callable before invoking it. This is commonly used to check optional callbacks before calling them.

followUps.question: Why is typeof safe to use on variables that may not exist?
followUps.answer: Normally, referencing a variable that was never declared throws a ReferenceError. But typeof has special handling: applying it to an undeclared variable returns the string 'undefined' instead of crashing. This makes typeof useful for safely probing whether a global or feature exists before relying on it.

question: What are truthy and falsy values in JavaScript?
directAnswer: In a boolean context, every value is either truthy or falsy. Falsy values are the small set that behave like false: false, 0, -0, 0n, '' (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN. Everything else is truthy, including non-empty strings, any number except zero, and all objects and arrays, even empty ones.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Truthiness is how a value is interpreted when JavaScript needs a boolean, such as in an if-statement. For example:
if ('hello') { ... }   // runs, non-empty string is truthy
if (0) { ... }         // skipped, 0 is falsy
if ([]) { ... }        // runs, empty array is still truthy
The value itself is not changed; it is just evaluated as true or false.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JavaScript frequently uses values directly in conditions instead of forcing you to write explicit comparisons. Truthy and falsy rules let you write concise checks like if (user) instead of if (user !== null && user !== undefined). This shorthand is convenient but requires knowing exactly which values count as falsy.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Whenever a value is used where a boolean is expected, the engine coerces it using fixed rules. It memorizes a short list of falsy values and treats everything else as truthy. Importantly, empty arrays and empty objects are truthy because they are still objects, which surprises many newcomers who expect them to be falsy.

whyImportant: Truthiness drives countless real conditions, default values, and short-circuit expressions. Misunderstanding it causes bugs like treating an empty array as 'no data' when it is actually truthy. Interviewers ask this to verify you know the falsy list by heart and avoid these common traps.
realWorldExample: You might guard code with if (username) to skip empty input, which works because an empty string is falsy. But if you write if (results) expecting an empty results array to skip, it will not, because empty arrays are truthy. You would need to check results.length instead. Knowing the rules prevents this mistake.

nestedTopics.title: The complete falsy list
nestedTopics.explanation: There are exactly eight falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n (BigInt zero), '' (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN. Memorizing this short list is the fastest way to reason about any condition, since everything not on it is truthy.

nestedTopics.title: Empty objects and arrays are truthy
nestedTopics.explanation: Both {} and [] are truthy because they are objects, regardless of being empty. To check whether an array has items you test array.length, and for objects you check Object.keys(obj).length. Relying on truthiness alone here is a common bug.

nestedTopics.title: Converting to a real boolean
nestedTopics.explanation: You can force a value to its boolean equivalent with Boolean(value) or the double-NOT trick !!value. Both return the actual true or false that the value would be treated as in a condition, which is useful for storing or returning a clean boolean.

followUps.question: Is an empty array truthy or falsy?
followUps.answer: An empty array is truthy. This surprises many developers because they expect 'empty' to mean falsy. But arrays are objects, and all objects are truthy regardless of their contents. To check whether an array actually contains elements, you should test array.length rather than the array itself in a condition.

followUps.question: What is the difference between checking if (value) and if (value != null)?
followUps.answer: if (value) is truthy-based, so it also skips for 0, empty strings, NaN, and false, not just null and undefined. if (value != null) uses loose equality to specifically catch only null and undefined while still allowing 0, empty strings, and false through. Use the second form when those falsy-but-valid values should be treated as present.

followUps.question: How do you convert any value to a boolean?
followUps.answer: You can use the Boolean function, like Boolean(value), or the shorthand double-NOT operator, like !!value. Both evaluate the value's truthiness and return the corresponding true or false. The double-NOT is popular because it is concise, while Boolean() is more explicit and readable for those less familiar with the trick.

question: What are template literals and what can they do?
directAnswer: Template literals are strings written with backticks instead of quotes. They let you embed variables and expressions directly using the ${} syntax, and they support multi-line strings without escape characters. They make string building far cleaner than the old approach of concatenating with the plus operator.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
A template literal is a string surrounded by backticks. For example:
const name = 'Lee';
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!`;   // 'Hello, Lee!'
const multi = `Line one
Line two`;             // real line break
The ${} parts can hold any JavaScript expression, not just variables.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Before template literals, building strings with variables meant clunky concatenation like 'Hello, ' + name + '!', which was hard to read and error-prone with spacing. Template literals, added in ES6, provide a clean, readable syntax for interpolation and multi-line text, which is one of the most-used modern features.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Inside backticks, the engine looks for ${} placeholders, evaluates the expression inside each one, converts the result to a string, and inserts it into the final string. Line breaks inside the backticks are preserved literally, so you get multi-line strings without \n. There is also an advanced form called tagged templates that lets a function process the parts.

whyImportant: Template literals appear in virtually all modern JavaScript, from logging to building HTML to formatting messages. Interviewers expect you to use them naturally and to understand they can hold full expressions. Comfort with them signals you write clean, contemporary code rather than relying on outdated concatenation.
realWorldExample: When generating a user notification you might write `You have ${count} new ${count === 1 ? 'message' : 'messages'}`. The expression handles both the value and the pluralization inline, producing readable output in a single line that would be messy and bug-prone with string concatenation.

nestedTopics.title: Embedding expressions, not just variables
nestedTopics.explanation: The ${} placeholder can contain any valid expression: arithmetic, function calls, ternaries, even nested template literals. For example `Total: ${price * quantity}` runs the calculation inline. This flexibility is what makes them so powerful.

nestedTopics.title: Multi-line strings
nestedTopics.explanation: Anything between the backticks keeps its line breaks, so you can write multi-line text or formatted blocks directly without inserting \n. This is especially handy for building small chunks of HTML or formatted console output.

nestedTopics.title: Tagged templates
nestedTopics.explanation: A tagged template lets you put a function name before the backticks, like tag`Hello ${name}`. That function receives the string pieces and the interpolated values separately, enabling custom processing such as escaping, localization, or styling. It is an advanced but useful capability.

followUps.question: Can you put a function call inside a template literal?
followUps.answer: Yes. The ${} placeholder accepts any expression, including function calls. For example `Hello, ${getName()}!` will invoke getName, convert its return value to a string, and embed it. This is a common and clean way to build dynamic strings without breaking out of the literal to do concatenation.

followUps.question: How do you write a multi-line string before template literals existed?
followUps.answer: Before template literals you either concatenated multiple strings with plus signs and explicit \n characters, like 'line one\n' + 'line two', or used backslash line continuations. Both were awkward and easy to get wrong. Template literals replaced all of that by simply preserving the line breaks you type between the backticks.

followUps.question: What is a tagged template literal used for?
followUps.answer: A tagged template lets a function intercept and process a template literal before it becomes a final string. The function receives an array of the static string parts and the interpolated values as separate arguments, so it can transform them however it wants. Common uses include safely escaping HTML, formatting numbers and dates, building SQL safely, and CSS-in-JS libraries like styled-components.

question: What is the difference between an arrow function and a regular function?
directAnswer: Arrow functions are a shorter syntax for writing functions, but the key difference is that they do not have their own this; they inherit it from the surrounding scope. They also lack their own arguments object and cannot be used as constructors. Regular functions get their own this based on how they are called, which makes them more flexible but sometimes harder to reason about.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
An arrow function uses the => syntax and is often more concise:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;            // arrow
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }    // regular
The arrow version can omit braces and the return keyword for single expressions, and it behaves differently with this.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Arrow functions were added in ES6 to provide shorter syntax and, more importantly, to solve the long-standing problem of this changing unexpectedly inside callbacks. By inheriting this from where they are defined, arrows make code like array callbacks and event handlers far less error-prone.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A regular function determines its this dynamically at call time: it could be the calling object, the global object, or undefined in strict mode. An arrow function has no this of its own, so any reference to this looks outward to the enclosing scope, captured at definition time. Arrows also have no arguments object, no prototype, and cannot be called with new.

whyImportant: The this difference is one of the most commonly tested topics because it trips up so many developers. Interviewers want to confirm you know when an arrow function is the right tool, such as in callbacks, and when a regular function is needed, such as object methods or constructors. Choosing wrong causes subtle this bugs.
realWorldExample: Inside a class method you might call setInterval and need to update an instance property. Using an arrow function as the callback means this still refers to the instance, so this.count++ works. A regular function callback there would have its own this (often undefined), breaking the update. This pattern shows up constantly in UI code.

nestedTopics.title: Lexical this
nestedTopics.explanation: Arrow functions capture this from the scope where they are written, not where they are called. This is called lexical this. It is the single biggest reason to choose an arrow, because it avoids the classic problem of this being lost inside nested callbacks.

nestedTopics.title: No arguments object
nestedTopics.explanation: Regular functions have a built-in arguments object holding all passed parameters. Arrow functions do not; if you need all arguments in an arrow you use rest parameters like (...args). This is a small but important practical difference.

nestedTopics.title: Cannot be constructors
nestedTopics.explanation: You cannot call an arrow function with the new keyword; doing so throws an error. Arrows have no prototype property and are not meant to create objects. For constructors you must use a regular function or a class.

followUps.question: Why should you avoid arrow functions as object methods?
followUps.answer: Because an arrow function inherits this from the surrounding scope rather than the object it belongs to. So inside an object method written as an arrow, this will not point to the object, often pointing to the global scope or undefined instead. For methods that need to access their object via this, use a regular function or shorthand method syntax.

followUps.question: Can an arrow function be used with the new keyword?
followUps.answer: No. Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors, so calling them with new throws a TypeError. They have no prototype property and no internal mechanism to build and return a new object. When you need a constructor you should use a regular function or, more commonly today, a class.

followUps.question: How do you access all arguments in an arrow function?
followUps.answer: Since arrow functions do not have their own arguments object, you use rest parameters. Writing the function as (...args) => { ... } collects all passed arguments into a real array named args, which you can iterate or process. This is actually cleaner than the old arguments object because args is a genuine array with array methods.

question: How do you create and access objects in JavaScript?
directAnswer: You usually create an object with object literal syntax using curly braces, listing key-value pairs. You access properties either with dot notation (obj.name) or bracket notation (obj['name']). Bracket notation is needed when the key is stored in a variable or contains special characters. Objects are the core way JavaScript groups related data and behavior.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
An object is a collection of named properties. The most common way to make one:
const user = { name: 'Ana', age: 28 };
user.name;        // 'Ana' (dot notation)
user['age'];      // 28 (bracket notation)
user.email = 'a@x.com';   // add a new property
Keys are strings (or symbols), and values can be anything.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Programs need a way to group related information together, like all the details of a user. Objects provide that structure, mapping descriptive keys to values. They are the foundation of JavaScript: arrays, functions, and most built-in features are objects under the hood.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When you use object literal syntax, the engine creates an object and stores each key-value pair. Dot notation looks up a property by a fixed name known at write time. Bracket notation evaluates whatever expression is inside the brackets to produce the key, which is why it works with variables. Accessing a missing property returns undefined rather than throwing an error.

whyImportant: Objects are everywhere in JavaScript, so fluency with creating and accessing them is fundamental. Interviewers check that you know both notations, when each is needed, and how to add, update, and remove properties. This is bedrock knowledge for working with data, configuration, and API responses.
realWorldExample: When you receive a JSON response from an API, it becomes a JavaScript object. You then read fields like response.user.name with dot notation, or use bracket notation like response[fieldName] when the field name is dynamic, such as iterating over a list of column keys. This is daily work in any application.

nestedTopics.title: Dot vs bracket notation
nestedTopics.explanation: Dot notation is cleaner and used when you know the exact key name. Bracket notation is required when the key is in a variable, is computed, or contains spaces or special characters, like obj['first name'] or obj[dynamicKey].

nestedTopics.title: Adding and removing properties
nestedTopics.explanation: You can add or update a property anytime by assigning to it, like obj.newKey = value. You remove a property with the delete operator, like delete obj.key. Objects are mutable, so these changes affect the object in place.

nestedTopics.title: Shorthand and computed keys
nestedTopics.explanation: ES6 lets you write { name } as shorthand when a variable and key share a name, and use computed keys like { [keyVar]: value } to set a property whose name comes from a variable. Both make object construction more concise.

followUps.question: When must you use bracket notation instead of dot notation?
followUps.answer: You must use bracket notation when the property key is not a fixed, valid identifier. That includes keys stored in variables (obj[keyName]), keys computed at runtime, keys containing spaces or hyphens (obj['user-id']), and purely numeric keys. Dot notation only works for hard-coded, syntactically valid names, so bracket notation is the flexible fallback.

followUps.question: What happens if you access a property that does not exist?
followUps.answer: JavaScript returns undefined rather than throwing an error. This is convenient but can hide typos, since misspelling a key simply gives undefined. If you go further and try to read a property of that undefined result, like obj.missing.subkey, then you do get an error. Optional chaining (obj?.missing?.subkey) safely handles such cases.

followUps.question: How do you remove a property from an object?
followUps.answer: You use the delete operator, like delete obj.propertyName. This removes the key and its value from the object entirely, so checking for it afterward returns undefined and it no longer appears in iteration. Note that delete is for object properties; to remove array elements you typically use methods like splice instead, since delete on arrays leaves a hole.

question: What are the most common array methods you should know?
directAnswer: The essentials include push and pop for adding and removing from the end, shift and unshift for the front, slice for copying a portion, splice for inserting or removing in place, indexOf and includes for searching, and the iteration methods forEach, map, filter, and reduce. Together these cover most everyday array work.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Arrays come with many built-in methods. A few examples:
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
nums.push(4);          // [1,2,3,4]
nums.includes(2);      // true
nums.map(n => n * 2);  // [2,4,6,8]
nums.filter(n => n > 2); // [3,4]
Each method either modifies the array or returns a new value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Arrays are the main ordered collection in JavaScript, so the language provides a rich set of methods to add, remove, search, and transform their contents without writing manual loops every time. These methods make code shorter, clearer, and less error-prone.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Some methods mutate the original array (push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse), changing it in place. Others are non-mutating and return a new array or value (slice, map, filter, reduce, concat, includes). Knowing which group a method belongs to is important because mutation can cause unexpected side effects in shared data.

whyImportant: Array manipulation is a daily task, and interviewers frequently test it both conceptually and in coding problems. Knowing the right method for each job, and especially which ones mutate versus return new arrays, demonstrates practical competence and helps you avoid subtle bugs from accidental mutation.
realWorldExample: Rendering a list of products on a page, you would map the data array into HTML elements, filter it to show only in-stock items, and maybe reduce it to compute a total price. These three methods alone power a huge amount of real UI and data work.

nestedTopics.title: Mutating vs non-mutating methods
nestedTopics.explanation: Mutating methods like push, splice, sort, and reverse change the original array. Non-mutating methods like map, filter, slice, and concat leave the original untouched and return something new. Preferring non-mutating methods makes code more predictable, especially in frameworks like React.

nestedTopics.title: slice vs splice
nestedTopics.explanation: These look similar but behave very differently. slice(start, end) returns a shallow copy of part of the array without changing it. splice(start, count, ...items) removes or inserts elements in place and mutates the original. Mixing them up is a classic mistake.

nestedTopics.title: Searching methods
nestedTopics.explanation: includes tells you whether a value is present and returns a boolean. indexOf returns the position or -1 if not found. find returns the first element matching a condition, and findIndex returns its index. Each suits a different searching need.

followUps.question: What is the difference between slice and splice?
followUps.answer: slice is non-mutating: it returns a shallow copy of a portion of the array between a start and end index, leaving the original array unchanged. splice is mutating: it changes the original array in place by removing, replacing, or inserting elements, and it returns the removed elements. A handy way to remember: slice keeps the original safe, splice surgically alters it.

followUps.question: Which array methods change the original array?
followUps.answer: The mutating methods are push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill, and copyWithin. They modify the array in place. Methods like map, filter, slice, concat, reduce, includes, indexOf, find, and join do not mutate; they return a new array or a value while leaving the original intact. Knowing this distinction helps prevent accidental side effects.

followUps.question: How do you check if an array contains a specific value?
followUps.answer: The simplest way is includes, like arr.includes(value), which returns true or false. If you need the position, use indexOf, which returns the index or -1 when not found. For more complex matching by a condition rather than an exact value, use find to get the matching element or some to get a boolean. The choice depends on whether you need existence, position, or the element itself.

question: What is the ternary operator and when should you use it?
directAnswer: The ternary operator is a compact one-line alternative to an if-else statement. It has the form condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. It evaluates the condition and returns one of two values. You should use it for simple, readable choices, especially when assigning a value, but avoid nesting it deeply because that hurts readability.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Often you need to pick between two values based on a condition, and writing a full if-else block just to assign a variable is verbose. The ternary provides a concise expression form for this, keeping simple either-or logic on a single readable line.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The engine evaluates the condition before the question mark. If it is truthy, the whole expression resolves to the value between ? and :. If it is falsy, it resolves to the value after the colon. Because it is an expression, you can use it inline anywhere a value is expected, such as inside template literals or function arguments.

whyImportant: The ternary is extremely common, particularly in frameworks like React for conditional rendering. Interviewers expect you to read and write it fluently and to know when it improves clarity versus when a plain if-statement is better. Misusing it with deep nesting is a readability red flag.
realWorldExample: In a UI you might render a label with `${isLoggedIn ? 'Logout' : 'Login'}` so the button text switches based on state. This is far cleaner than an if-else block for a single value, which is why ternaries are everywhere in component code.

nestedTopics.title: Ternary as an expression
nestedTopics.explanation: Unlike an if-statement, the ternary returns a value, so you can use it directly in assignments, return statements, template literals, and function calls. This is its main advantage and the reason it shows up inline so often.

nestedTopics.title: Avoiding nested ternaries
nestedTopics.explanation: Chaining multiple ternaries together quickly becomes hard to read, like a ? b : c ? d : e. For more than one condition it is usually clearer to use an if-else chain or a switch. Keep ternaries to simple two-way choices.

nestedTopics.title: Ternary vs short-circuit operators
nestedTopics.explanation: For providing a default value you often see || or ?? instead of a ternary, like name || 'Guest'. The ternary is better when the two outcomes are genuinely different values, while short-circuit operators are better for simple fallback defaults.

followUps.question: Can a ternary operator return nothing or just run side effects?
followUps.answer: Technically you can put function calls in each branch, but the ternary is designed to produce a value, not to run statements for side effects. Using it purely to execute actions instead of choosing a value is considered poor style. For side-effect logic, a normal if-statement communicates intent more clearly and is easier to read.

followUps.question: When is an if-else better than a ternary?
followUps.answer: An if-else is better when the logic is complex, when each branch runs multiple statements, or when there are more than two outcomes. Ternaries shine for short, single-value choices. If you find yourself nesting ternaries or adding line breaks to make one readable, that is a strong signal to switch to an if-else or switch statement instead.

followUps.question: How is the ternary used in React for conditional rendering?
followUps.answer: In React JSX you cannot use if-statements directly inside the markup, so the ternary is the standard way to choose between two pieces of UI. For example, {isLoading ? <Spinner /> : <Content />} renders one component or the other based on state. This inline, value-returning nature is exactly why ternaries are so prevalent in React code.

question: What is the difference between for...of and for...in loops?
directAnswer: for...of iterates over the values of an iterable, like the elements of an array or characters of a string. for...in iterates over the keys (property names) of an object, including array indexes. As a rule, use for...of for arrays and other iterables, and for...in for plain object properties.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JavaScript needed a clean way to iterate object properties (for...in, present since early versions) and later a clean way to iterate over the values of iterables like arrays, strings, maps, and sets (for...of, added in ES6). They serve genuinely different purposes, which is why both exist.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: for...in walks the enumerable property keys of an object, including inherited ones from the prototype chain, and always yields keys as strings. for...of uses the iterator protocol to walk the values produced by any iterable. Because for...in includes inherited keys and order is not guaranteed for objects, it is not recommended for arrays.

whyImportant: Choosing the wrong loop is a frequent beginner bug, especially using for...in on arrays and getting string indexes or inherited properties. Interviewers ask this to confirm you understand iterables versus enumerable keys and know the correct tool for each data structure.
realWorldExample: When you need to sum the numbers in an array you use for...of to get each value directly. When you need to print every key and value of a config object you use for...in to walk its property names. Using the wrong one, like for...in on an array, can introduce inherited keys and subtle bugs.

nestedTopics.title: for...in includes inherited keys
nestedTopics.explanation: for...in iterates over all enumerable properties, including those inherited through the prototype chain. This can surprise you with unexpected keys. If you only want the object's own keys, guard with Object.hasOwn(obj, key) or iterate Object.keys(obj) instead.

nestedTopics.title: for...of needs an iterable
nestedTopics.explanation: for...of only works on iterables: arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, and similar. It does not work directly on plain objects, which are not iterable by default. Trying for...of on a plain object throws an error unless you convert it, for example with Object.entries.

nestedTopics.title: Iterating object entries cleanly
nestedTopics.explanation: A modern way to loop a plain object's keys and values is for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(obj)). This combines for...of with Object.entries to get both pieces at once, avoiding the pitfalls of for...in.

followUps.question: Why should you avoid for...in on arrays?
followUps.answer: Because for...in iterates over keys, not values, so on an array you get the indexes as strings ('0', '1', ...) rather than the elements. Worse, it includes any enumerable properties added to the array or its prototype, which can introduce unexpected entries, and the iteration order is not strictly guaranteed. For arrays, for...of (for values) or a standard indexed for loop is safer and clearer.

followUps.question: How do you loop over both keys and values of an object?
followUps.answer: The cleanest modern approach is to combine Object.entries with for...of: for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(obj)) { ... }. Object.entries returns an array of [key, value] pairs, and destructuring in the loop gives you both directly. Alternatively, you can use for...in to get keys and look up obj[key] for values, but the entries approach avoids inherited-key pitfalls.

followUps.question: Can you use for...of directly on a plain object?
followUps.answer: No, not directly, because plain objects are not iterable and for...of relies on the iterator protocol. Attempting it throws a TypeError. To iterate an object with for...of, you first convert it to an iterable form using Object.keys, Object.values, or Object.entries, each returning an array you can then loop over.

question: What is NaN and how do you check for it?
directAnswer: NaN stands for 'Not a Number' and is a special numeric value that represents an invalid or undefined mathematical result, like dividing zero by zero or parsing a non-numeric string. The tricky part is that NaN is not equal to anything, including itself, so you check for it with Number.isNaN(value) rather than a normal comparison.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
NaN is a value of type number that means a numeric operation failed. Examples:
Number('hello')   // NaN
0 / 0             // NaN
Math.sqrt(-1)     // NaN
typeof NaN        // 'number' (ironically)
It signals that something that should have produced a number did not.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: When a calculation cannot produce a meaningful number, the language needs a way to represent that failure without crashing. NaN provides that, following the IEEE floating-point standard. It lets numeric code keep running while clearly marking results that are invalid.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: By the floating-point standard, NaN is defined as unequal to every value, including itself, so NaN === NaN is false. This means you cannot detect it with equality. Instead, Number.isNaN(value) reliably returns true only for actual NaN. There is also a global isNaN function, but it coerces its argument first, which can give misleading results.

whyImportant: NaN bugs are sneaky because they propagate silently through calculations, turning a whole result into NaN without an error. Interviewers ask this to ensure you know why it cannot be compared normally and how to detect it properly, which is essential for robust numeric and data-processing code.
realWorldExample: When parsing user input like a price field, Number(input) returns NaN if the input is not numeric. If you then do arithmetic with it, the result becomes NaN and silently corrupts your totals. Checking with Number.isNaN before using the value lets you catch invalid input and show an error instead.

nestedTopics.title: NaN is never equal to anything
nestedTopics.explanation: Because of the floating-point standard, NaN === NaN is false, and so is any other comparison with NaN. This is the single most surprising fact about it and the reason normal equality checks fail to detect it.

nestedTopics.title: Number.isNaN vs global isNaN
nestedTopics.explanation: The global isNaN coerces its argument to a number first, so isNaN('hello') is true even though 'hello' is not NaN itself. Number.isNaN does no coercion and returns true only for the actual NaN value, making it the reliable choice.

nestedTopics.title: How NaN appears
nestedTopics.explanation: NaN commonly results from failed conversions like Number('abc'), invalid math like 0/0 or Math.sqrt(-1), and operations involving undefined. Recognizing these sources helps you guard against it before it spreads through your calculations.

followUps.question: Why is NaN === NaN false?
followUps.answer: It is by design, following the IEEE 754 floating-point standard that JavaScript adopts. NaN represents an undefined or unrepresentable result, and since two such invalid results are not meaningfully 'the same', the standard defines NaN as not equal to anything, including another NaN. This is why you must use Number.isNaN or Object.is to detect it rather than an equality comparison.

followUps.question: What is the difference between isNaN and Number.isNaN?
followUps.answer: The global isNaN first coerces its argument to a number and then checks, so it returns true for many non-NaN values like isNaN('hello') or isNaN(undefined) because they coerce to NaN. Number.isNaN performs no coercion and returns true only when the value is literally the NaN value. Number.isNaN is the safer, more predictable choice and should be preferred.

followUps.question: What type is NaN?
followUps.answer: Ironically, typeof NaN returns 'number'. Even though its name means 'Not a Number', it is technically a numeric value that represents an invalid number, so it belongs to the number type. This is consistent with the idea that NaN is the result of a numeric operation that failed, so it stays within the numeric domain rather than becoming some other type.

question: What are some common string methods in JavaScript?
directAnswer: Frequently used string methods include length to get size, toUpperCase and toLowerCase for case changes, trim to remove whitespace, slice and substring to extract parts, indexOf and includes to search, replace and replaceAll to substitute text, and split to break a string into an array. Strings are immutable, so these methods return new strings rather than changing the original.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Strings come with many built-in helpers. Examples:
const s = '  Hello World  ';
s.trim();              // 'Hello World'
s.toUpperCase();       // '  HELLO WORLD  '
s.includes('World');   // true
s.split(' ');          // ['', '', 'Hello', 'World', '', '']
Each returns a value without modifying s.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Text processing is one of the most common tasks in programming, so JavaScript provides a rich set of string methods to search, transform, extract, and reformat text without writing manual character loops. This makes everyday work like formatting and validation concise.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Because strings are primitive and immutable, no method ever changes the original string; each returns a brand new string (or another value like a number or array). When you call a method on a string, JavaScript temporarily wraps it in a String object to access the method, runs it, and returns the result, discarding the wrapper.

whyImportant: String manipulation shows up in nearly every application and in many coding interview problems. Knowing the right methods and remembering that strings are immutable helps you write correct, efficient text-handling code and avoids the mistake of expecting a method to modify a string in place.
realWorldExample: When normalizing user input for a search, you might chain methods: input.trim().toLowerCase() to remove stray spaces and unify case before comparing. When parsing a CSV line you use split(',') to turn it into an array of fields. These small operations are constant in real code.

nestedTopics.title: Strings are immutable
nestedTopics.explanation: You cannot change a character of an existing string in place. Methods that seem to modify a string actually return a new one. So to 'change' a string you reassign the variable to the method's result, like s = s.trim().

nestedTopics.title: slice vs substring
nestedTopics.explanation: Both extract part of a string, but they handle negative indexes differently. slice accepts negative numbers to count from the end, while substring treats negatives as zero. slice is generally the more flexible and commonly recommended choice.

nestedTopics.title: split and join
nestedTopics.explanation: split breaks a string into an array based on a separator, and the array method join does the reverse, combining an array into a string with a chosen separator. Together they are a common pattern for transforming text, such as reversing words in a sentence.

followUps.question: Why can't you change a character of a string directly?
followUps.answer: Because strings are immutable primitives in JavaScript. Attempting something like str[0] = 'X' silently does nothing (or throws in strict mode) and leaves the string unchanged. To produce a modified string you create a new one, for example by slicing and concatenating or by splitting into an array, changing it, and joining back. The original string itself can never be altered.

followUps.question: What is the difference between replace and replaceAll?
followUps.answer: replace by default only substitutes the first match of a string pattern (though with a global regular expression it can replace all). replaceAll substitutes every occurrence of the pattern without needing a regex flag, which is clearer and less error-prone. So for replacing all occurrences of a plain substring, replaceAll is the simplest and most readable choice.

followUps.question: How do you convert a string into an array?
followUps.answer: You use the split method, passing a separator that determines where to break. For example, 'a,b,c'.split(',') produces ['a', 'b', 'c'], and 'word'.split('') produces an array of individual characters. Splitting on an empty string gives characters, while splitting on spaces or commas gives words or fields. The array can then be processed with array methods and rejoined with join if needed.

question: What is JSON and how do you use JSON.parse and JSON.stringify?
directAnswer: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text format for storing and exchanging data, based on JavaScript object syntax. JSON.stringify converts a JavaScript object into a JSON string, useful for storing or sending data. JSON.parse does the reverse, turning a JSON string back into a JavaScript object. Together they let you move structured data between systems.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different systems, like a browser and a server, need a common, language-neutral way to exchange structured data. JSON became that standard because it is simple, human-readable, and maps cleanly to objects and arrays. Almost every web API speaks JSON.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: JSON.stringify walks the object and produces a text representation following JSON rules: double-quoted keys, supported value types only, and no functions or undefined (those are dropped or turned to null). JSON.parse reads such text, validates it, and reconstructs the corresponding JavaScript values. Invalid JSON passed to parse throws an error, so it is often wrapped in try-catch.

whyImportant: Virtually all data exchange with servers, APIs, and storage uses JSON, so these two methods are part of everyday work. Interviewers ask about them to confirm you understand serialization, the limits of JSON (no functions, no undefined), and pitfalls like deep-copy misuse and parse errors.
realWorldExample: When saving user settings to localStorage, which only stores strings, you call JSON.stringify on the settings object before saving and JSON.parse when reading it back to restore the object. Similarly, fetching from an API returns a JSON string that you parse into a usable object. This round trip is extremely common.

nestedTopics.title: What JSON cannot represent
nestedTopics.explanation: JSON has no support for functions, undefined, symbols, or dates as real types. When stringifying, functions and undefined are omitted from objects, and dates are converted to strings. You must account for this when serializing complex objects.

nestedTopics.title: Pretty-printing output
nestedTopics.explanation: JSON.stringify accepts extra arguments: a replacer to filter or transform values, and a spacing number or string for indentation. For example JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2) produces nicely indented, human-readable output, which is handy for logging and debugging.

nestedTopics.title: Using it for deep copies (with caveats)
nestedTopics.explanation: A quick deep copy trick is JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)). It works for plain data but silently loses functions, undefined, dates become strings, and it fails on circular references. For reliable deep copies, structuredClone is the modern alternative.

followUps.question: What happens to functions and undefined when you stringify an object?
followUps.answer: They are not preserved because JSON has no concept of functions or undefined. When you call JSON.stringify on an object, any property whose value is a function or undefined is simply dropped from the resulting string. Inside an array, however, undefined and functions are converted to null to keep positions intact. This is why JSON round-tripping is unsafe for objects that contain behavior or undefined values.

followUps.question: What happens if JSON.parse receives invalid JSON?
followUps.answer: It throws a SyntaxError and stops execution at that point. Because data from networks, files, or user input can be malformed, you should wrap JSON.parse in a try-catch block to handle the error gracefully instead of letting it crash your program. Common causes of invalid JSON include trailing commas, single quotes instead of double quotes, and incomplete or truncated responses.

followUps.question: Why is JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) not a perfect deep copy?
followUps.answer: Because the JSON round trip can only represent JSON-compatible data. It loses functions and undefined, converts Date objects to plain strings, drops symbols, and throws an error on circular references. It also cannot preserve special types like Map, Set, or class instances. For a faithful deep copy of plain and many built-in types, the modern structuredClone function is a better choice, though it still cannot clone functions.

question: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
directAnswer: A function declaration uses the function keyword followed by a name, like function greet(){}, and is fully hoisted so you can call it before it appears in the code. A function expression assigns a function to a variable, like const greet = function(){}, and is not callable before that line runs. The main practical difference is hoisting behavior.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JavaScript treats functions as values, so it allows both a statement form (declaration) and an expression form (assigning a function to a variable). The expression form is useful for passing functions around, defining them conditionally, or creating them inline, while declarations are convenient for top-level reusable functions.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Function declarations are hoisted entirely, name and body, so they are available throughout their scope even before the line they are written on. Function expressions follow the hoisting rules of the variable they are assigned to: with const or let, the variable is in the temporal dead zone until its line runs, so calling the function early throws an error.

whyImportant: This distinction directly affects whether your code works depending on where you call a function. Interviewers use it to test your understanding of hoisting and how functions are treated as first-class values. Picking the right form, and knowing why one fails when called early, is practical everyday knowledge.
realWorldExample: If you organize a file with helper functions at the bottom and call them at the top, declarations work because they are hoisted. But if those helpers were written as const expressions, calling them at the top would throw a ReferenceError. Knowing this guides how you structure and order your code.

nestedTopics.title: Hoisting differences
nestedTopics.explanation: Declarations are hoisted with their full body and can be invoked before their position in the source. Expressions are only as available as their variable, so const and let expressions cannot be called before assignment. This is the core behavioral difference.

nestedTopics.title: Named function expressions
nestedTopics.explanation: A function expression can have its own name, like const f = function inner(){}. The name inner is only visible inside the function and is useful for recursion and clearer stack traces during debugging, while f is how you call it from outside.

nestedTopics.title: Functions as first-class values
nestedTopics.explanation: Because functions are values, you can store them in variables, pass them as arguments, and return them from other functions. The expression form makes this nature explicit and underpins callbacks, higher-order functions, and much of JavaScript's flexibility.

followUps.question: Can you call a function expression before it is defined?
followUps.answer: No, not if it is assigned with const or let. The variable holding the function is hoisted but stays in the temporal dead zone until its assignment runs, so calling it earlier throws a ReferenceError. Only function declarations, which are fully hoisted with their body, can be safely called before the line they appear on. This is the most important practical difference between the two forms.

followUps.question: What is an anonymous function?
followUps.answer: An anonymous function is one without a name, typically created as a function expression or arrow function and used inline, such as a callback passed to setTimeout or array methods. For example, arr.map(function(x){ return x * 2; }) uses an anonymous function. They are convenient for one-off use, though giving functions names can improve debugging because the name appears in stack traces.

followUps.question: Why might you choose a function expression over a declaration?
followUps.answer: Function expressions are useful when you want to treat a function as a value: assigning it conditionally, passing it as an argument, returning it from another function, or defining it inline as a callback. They also let you create functions only when needed, and with const they prevent accidental redeclaration. Declarations are better for clearly named, reusable functions that you want available throughout their scope regardless of order.

question: What are default parameters in functions?
directAnswer: Default parameters let you specify a fallback value for a function argument that is used when the caller does not pass that argument or passes undefined. You write them right in the parameter list, like function greet(name = 'Guest'). This avoids manual checks inside the function and makes the expected defaults clear at a glance.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Before ES6, developers handled missing arguments with verbose checks like name = name || 'Guest', which had bugs when valid falsy values were passed. Default parameters, added in ES6, provide a clean, built-in way to set fallbacks directly in the signature, making functions safer and more readable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When a function is called, each parameter that receives undefined (either because it was omitted or explicitly passed as undefined) takes its default value instead. Crucially, passing null does not trigger the default; only undefined does. Defaults can also be expressions or reference earlier parameters, and they are evaluated at call time.

whyImportant: Default parameters make functions more robust and self-documenting. Interviewers ask about them to verify you know the modern, correct way to handle optional arguments and the subtle rule that only undefined, not null or other falsy values, triggers the default. This prevents a common class of bugs.
realWorldExample: A function that fetches data might accept an options object with a default like function fetchData(url, retries = 3). Callers who do not care about retries simply omit it and get a sensible default, while those who need a different value pass it. This keeps the API flexible and clean.

nestedTopics.title: Only undefined triggers the default
nestedTopics.explanation: The default value is used only when the argument is undefined, which happens when it is omitted or explicitly undefined. Passing null, 0, false, or an empty string does not trigger the default; those values pass through as given. This is an important distinction from the old || pattern.

nestedTopics.title: Defaults can be expressions
nestedTopics.explanation: A default does not have to be a constant. It can be any expression, including a function call or a reference to an earlier parameter, like function box(w, h = w). The expression is evaluated each time the default is needed, at call time.

nestedTopics.title: Comparison with the old || pattern
nestedTopics.explanation: The older approach, x = x || defaultValue, mistakenly replaces any falsy value (0, '', false) with the default. Default parameters fix this by only applying when the argument is undefined, making them safer for arguments where falsy values are legitimate.

followUps.question: Does passing null trigger a default parameter?
followUps.answer: No. Default parameters apply only when the argument is undefined, which means it was either omitted or explicitly set to undefined. Passing null is treated as an intentional value, so the default does not kick in and the parameter receives null. This is a common gotcha: if you want null to also fall back to a default, you need an explicit check inside the function.

followUps.question: Can a default parameter reference another parameter?
followUps.answer: Yes, as long as the referenced parameter comes earlier in the list. For example, function makeRange(start, end = start + 10) uses start to compute the default for end. The defaults are evaluated left to right at call time, so a later parameter can depend on an earlier one, but not the other way around since the earlier parameter would not yet have a value.

followUps.question: Why are default parameters better than the x = x || default pattern?
followUps.answer: The old || pattern replaces any falsy argument with the default, which breaks when 0, an empty string, or false are valid inputs, because those would be wrongly overridden. Default parameters only apply when the argument is undefined, so legitimate falsy values pass through untouched. They are also clearer, appearing right in the function signature, which documents the expected defaults to anyone reading the code.

question: What is the difference between parameters and arguments?
directAnswer: Parameters are the named variables listed in a function's definition, acting as placeholders. Arguments are the actual values you pass to the function when you call it. So parameters are part of the function declaration, while arguments are the real data supplied at call time. People often use the terms loosely, but interviewers like to see you know the precise distinction.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Functions need a way to accept variable input. Parameters define the shape of that input as named placeholders, and arguments are how callers fill those placeholders with real values. This separation lets the same function work with many different inputs.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When you call a function, JavaScript assigns each argument to the corresponding parameter in order. If you pass fewer arguments than parameters, the missing ones become undefined (or use defaults). If you pass more, the extras are ignored by name but still accessible via the arguments object (in regular functions) or rest parameters.

whyImportant: This is a fundamentals-and-vocabulary check. Interviewers want to confirm you use the terms correctly and understand how values flow into functions, including what happens with missing or extra arguments. Precise vocabulary signals clear thinking, and the mechanics matter for handling flexible function inputs.
realWorldExample: When documenting or discussing a function with teammates, saying 'the function takes two parameters' versus 'I passed the wrong argument' communicates clearly. In code, understanding that extra arguments are still capturable via rest parameters lets you write flexible functions like a sum that accepts any number of values.

nestedTopics.title: Too few or too many arguments
nestedTopics.explanation: JavaScript does not enforce argument counts. Missing arguments become undefined (or use defaults), and extra arguments are simply not bound to named parameters, though they remain reachable through rest parameters or the arguments object.

nestedTopics.title: The arguments object
nestedTopics.explanation: Inside a regular (non-arrow) function, arguments is an array-like object holding every argument passed, regardless of the declared parameters. It is a legacy way to access all inputs, now largely replaced by rest parameters.

nestedTopics.title: Rest parameters
nestedTopics.explanation: Rest parameters, written as ...args, collect any remaining arguments into a real array. They are the modern, cleaner alternative to the arguments object and work in arrow functions too, making variable-arity functions easy to write.

followUps.question: What happens if you call a function with fewer arguments than parameters?
followUps.answer: The parameters that did not receive an argument are set to undefined, unless they have default values, in which case the defaults are used. JavaScript does not throw an error for missing arguments, so the function still runs. This is why it is common to provide default parameters or check for undefined when a function can be called with optional arguments.

followUps.question: What is the arguments object?
followUps.answer: The arguments object is an array-like collection available inside regular (non-arrow) functions that contains all the arguments passed, even ones not matched to named parameters. You can access them by index like arguments[0], but it is not a true array, so it lacks methods like map.
